extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, compositors, and typesetters producing publications for an academic press (University of Chicago Press) or similar publishing houses
extracted.subtask_description: A codified manual of typographical and editorial rules governing composition, capitalization, italicization, quotations, punctuation, divisions, footnotes, indexing, tabular work, technical terms, and specimen type usage for publications of an academic press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize proper nouns and derived adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns (e.g., George, America, Elizabethan, French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names (e.g., to boycott, to christianize). Examples supplied. (See 53.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize epithets used as substitutes for proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize epithets used as substitutes for proper names, or affixed to a name (e.g., the Pretender, Richard the Lion-hearted, Alexander the Great).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given; treat the epithet as part of the proper name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize particles in French names only when standing alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize particles in French names ('le', 'la', 'de', 'du') when standing without a Christian name or title preceding; but not when preceded by such name or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Bossu, La Rochelle, De Coligny, Du Maurier — but Miguel de la Torre, Thomas d'Aubigné, Monsieur de la Torre. Guidance shows exceptions and comparable forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize Van in Dutch names; don't capitalize von in German names
rubrics_metrics.description: Always capitalize 'Van' in Dutch names; never capitalize 'von' in German names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stephen Van Rensselaer; Hugo von Martius, von Dobschütz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize generic terms that are part of geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms that form an organic part of geographical names (e.g., Atlantic Ocean, Gulf of Mexico, Mississippi River, Rocky Mountains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists of common geographic generics provided; contrasted with cases where these terms are descriptive only (see next rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not capitalize generic geographical descriptors used descriptively
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize words of the geographic class when simply added by way of description to the specific name, without forming an organic part of such name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara, the island of Madagascar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize listed geographic words in singular form only when immediately following a name
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words (Archipelago, Gap, Ocean, County, Mountain, River, etc.) should be capitalized in singular form only when immediately following a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides long lists organized by form and position (singular following name; singular either before or after name; plural before the name). Use these lists as a reference for capitalization of geographic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize adjectives/nouns used to designate definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize adjectives and nouns used singly or in conjunction to distinguish definite regions or parts of the world and terms applied to groups of states (e.g., Old World, Western Hemisphere, the Orient, Gulf states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But do not as a rule capitalize adjectives derived from such names or nouns designating direction or compass point when used generically (e.g., oriental customs, northern Europe, the southern states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize generic terms for political divisions when part of name
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic political-division terms when they are organic parts of the name (e.g., Holy Roman Empire, French Republic, United Kingdom, Cook County).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: capitalize when used with 'of' as integral part for minor U.S. administrative subdivisions (Department of the Lakes) and when used singly as the accepted designation for a specific division (the Union, the States). Do not capitalize when generic or paraphrastic (the empire, the state).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize numbered political or municipal divisions when they form part of official names (e.g., Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-reference to rule 100 for more on numbered divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, buildings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, blocks, buildings, and similar specific places (e.g., Drexel Avenue, Lincoln Park, Trafalgar Square, Lakeside Building, White House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general designations of buildings (courthouse, post-office, library) except in connection with a specific place name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of political parties, denominations, schools, and adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of political parties, religious denominations or sects, philosophical, literary and artistic schools, and their adherents (e.g., Republican, Catholic, Romantic movement, Symbolic school).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these words when used in a general sense (e.g., republican form of government, socialism as an economic panacea). Examples and anti-patterns provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize monastic orders and members
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members (e.g., Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No extended guidance beyond examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize official titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper (official) titles of social, religious, educational, political, commercial, and industrial organizations and institutions (e.g., Union League Club, Smithsonian Institution, State University of Iowa, The Macmillan Company).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms used to designate a class or when standing alone; exceptions when the word is consistently used in place of the true name or to avoid ambiguity. Examples and notes (see 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of legislative, judicial, and administrative bodies when specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of legislative, judiciary, and administrative bodies and governmental departments and branches when specifically applied (e.g., Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general or paraphrastic references (the national assembly, the legislature of the state).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize ordinals for dynasties, sessions, regiments, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments, and similar connections (e.g., the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Fifty-third Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 100 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize commonly accepted appellations for historical epochs and geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize commonly accepted appellations for historical epochs, literary periods, and geological ages and strata (e.g., Renaissance, Middle Ages, Pleistocene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'age' is capitalized only where failure to do so would result in ambiguity (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names for important events
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names for important events (e.g., Thirty Years' War, Revolution, Battle of Gettysburg, Louisiana Purchase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for wars, battles, treaties, purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize political alliances and terms that have acquired significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political alliances and terms from history that have become significant designations for parties, movements, etc. (e.g., Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses, the Roundheads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 9 about capitalizing schools/movements; examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize conventions, congresses, expositions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of conventions, congresses, expositions, and similar gatherings (e.g., Council of Nicaea, Fifteenth International Congress of Criminology, Chicago World's Fair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as formal titles for events; ordinal and descriptive parts capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, and bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills, etc. (e.g., Treaty of Verdun, Declaration of Independence, Fourteenth Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on when 'the Constitution' may be capitalized when standing alone (U.S. context) but typically not for other states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the names of creeds and confessions of faith (e.g., Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exception references for ante-Nicene usage (see 203, 208).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize civic and ecclesiastical feast-days
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize civic and ecclesiastical feast-days and named holidays (e.g., Fourth of July, Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Easter, Passover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: 'sabbath' as a day of rest is not capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize titles preceding names and certain degrees after names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles (civil and military) preceding names, and academic degrees in abbreviated form following the name; titles of honor or nobility referring to specific persons are capitalized (e.g., Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Timothy Dwight, D.D., LL.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize titles following the name (McKinley, president of the United States). Titles standing alone without name are not capitalized except certain high offices referring to existing incumbents (the President, the King) — see exceptions. Examples and contextual guidance provided (see 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize certain abbreviations without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.; set them without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules 22, 103, 106 and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize one-letter abbreviations (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize abbreviations consisting of one letter only, except in case of units of measurement and minor literary subdivisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: R.V. (Revised Version), C. (centigrade), H.P. (horse-power), A.U. (Angström units). See rules 54, 55, 210 for related exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names and adjectives referring to the Supreme Being and Trinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns and adjectives used to designate the Supreme Being or any member of the Christian Trinity (e.g., the Almighty, Father, Son, Holy Ghost) and pronouns referring to them when not closely preceded or followed by a distinctive name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derived expressions (God's fatherhood, messianic). Use capitalization in personified or reverent contexts; examples and exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize words with acquired or limited special meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words which have an acquired, limited, or special meaning in context (e.g., the Doctor's degree; a report of the Master in chancery; a Bachelor's hood; a Freshman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic forms (e.g., the doctorate, a master in chancery) where capitalization no longer indicates a special meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize personified 'Nature' and similar abstract personifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Nature' and similar abstract ideas when personified (e.g., 'Nature wields her scepter mercilessly').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include personified abstractions in literature and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'Father' for church Fathers and 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders where ambiguity would result
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Father' when used for church fathers and 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders when the meaning otherwise would be ambiguous (e.g., the Fathers, the Reformers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize in broader contexts (the church reformers of the fifteenth century). Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'church' in properly cited national bodies and building names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the word 'church' in properly cited titles of nationally organized bodies or when forming part of the name of a particular edifice (e.g., Church of Rome, Fifth Avenue Baptist Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone in universal or national senses (the church = organized Christianity), except where emphasis is desired to mark Church/State antithesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names for the Bible and other sacred books and collective designations (e.g., Holy Scriptures, Word of God, Koran, Vedas, Apocrypha).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (biblical, scriptural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize versions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of Bible versions (e.g., King James's Version, Authorized Version, Revised Version, Septuagint (LXX)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations and conventional short-forms given (A.V., R.V.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize books and divisions of sacred texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize book names and divisions of the Bible and other sacred books (e.g., Old Testament, Pentateuch, Exodus, Psalms, Gospel of Luke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms like 'book', 'gospel', 'epistle' in certain contexts (the five books of Moses, the gospels and epistles). See rule 60 and 41 for titles guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize named biblical parables
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize named biblical parables when referenced by their accepted titles (e.g., the Parable of the Prodigal Son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short rule with example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize miscellaneous sacred designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize miscellaneous sacred designations and names associated with biblical narrative (e.g., Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Psalmist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided showing conventional capitalization in ecclesiastical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and in poetry the first word of each line
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, and in poetry the first word of each line (except in Greek and Latin poetry where only the first word of a paragraph is capitalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in English and in Greek/Latin poetry illustrating the exception. Cross-reference to rule 35 and 131 for quotes/colons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize the first word after a colon only in independent passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when introducing a complete passage or sentence which would have independent meaning, as in summarizations and quotations not closely connected with what precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: capitalize after a colon when it has the weight of 'as follows' or when a full sentence follows; do not capitalize when the colon introduces a phrase dependent upon the preceding clause or a brief quotation closely connected with the preceding text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first words in enumerated sections depending on clause structure
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, capitalize the first word in sections of enumeration if any link contains two or more distinct clauses (not enclosed in parentheses) separated by semicolon, colon, or period, unless all are dependent on the same term preceding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show when enumerated points begin with capitals vs. lower-case dependent fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize nouns followed by numerals indicating sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, capitalize nouns followed by a numeral — particularly a capital Roman numeral — indicating their order in a sequence (e.g., Room 16, Vol. I, Act I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions of publications (sec. 4, scene i, art. iii, chap. 2(ii), p. 7(vii)). See rule 37 and no.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first word of a cited speech in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a cited speech (thought) in direct discourse, whether preceded by a colon or comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show punctuation before quotes and capitalization of initial quoted words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions, capitalize the first words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' (e.g., Whereas, It has pleased God...; Resolved, That...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting conventions for resolutions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' when used in exclamatory address (e.g., 'O Lord!', 'Oh, that I were home again!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 117 for related punctuation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize principal words in English titles of publications and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications (books, periodicals), their divisions, subjects of lectures, and specified heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: some journals (e.g., Botanical Gazette) capitalize only first words and proper names for bibliographies; guidance for caps-and-small-caps and italic center-heads; see rules 41 and 279-283 for table heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize appropriately in foreign titles following language conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles, capitalize according to the conventions of the language: Latin — proper nouns and derived adjectives; French/Italian/Spanish/Scandinavian — proper nouns but not derived adjectives; German/Danish — capitalize all nouns; Dutch — capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each language illustrating correct capitalization patterns in titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat definite articles as part of newspaper/magazine titles as a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When mentioning titles of newspapers and magazines, do not as a rule treat the definite article as part of the title (e.g., the Chicago Tribune, the School Review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General practice: omit 'The' as part of the title in prose references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts (MS, MSS) when cited (e.g., Codex Bernensis, Cod. Canonicianus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 60 for manuscript treatments in biblical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize all nouns in hyphenated compounds in titles when main words are capitalized
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds (e.g., 'Twentieth-Century Progress').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize other components when they are not nouns (e.g., Fifty-first Street, 'Lives of Well-known Authors').

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize scientific (Latin) names of higher taxa but not English derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological matter, capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera, but not their English derivatives (e.g., Cotylosauria but cotylosaurs; Felidae but felids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Species names: capitalize species derived from persons or generic names in botanical/zoological matter; in geological and medical matter species names are never capitalized. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes (e.g., Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No extended guidance; example list provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of celestial bodies (selected terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, capitalize the names of the bodies of our solar system (except 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', 'stars') such as the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use context conventions for capitalization of celestial names and common nouns referring to astronomical objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize University of Chicago internal divisions and officers in official work
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in official work dealing with its administration or curricula (e.g., the School of Education, Department of Anthropology, the Board of Trustees, the President).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In informal or generic senses use lower-case (the department, the faculty); examples illustrate exceptions (Van Husen Scholarship vs. the scholarship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use capitals and small capitals for date lines, salutatory phrase, signature and residence lines in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Capitals and Small Capitals for the names of town and state in the date line and the salutatory phrase at the beginning, and the signature and residence at the end of letters; format guidance for indentation and type size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911; My dear Mr. Smith:; Charles W. Scott; Harvard University, Cambridge, Mass. Layout rules and indentation guidance provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize headings like 'Whereas' in resolutions, 'Note' in notes, 'Section' in constitutions/by-laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions capitalize 'Whereas'; in notes use 'Note.' followed by period and dash; in constitutions and by-laws capitalize 'Section' when introducing paragraphs and followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convention: abbreviate 'Section' after the first occurrence (Section 1. ... Sec 2. ...). Example formatting provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set A.M./P.M. and B.C./A.D. in small capitals without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M., and B.C. and A.D. in small capitals and without a space between letters (e.g., 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules 22, 103, 106, 219.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small initial letter for words whose origin as proper names has become generic and for verbs derived from proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial for words of common usage originally proper names whose origin is obscured (e.g., utopia, bohemian, boycott, italicize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show verbs derived from names and nouns that have become genericized (see rule 53).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small initial letter for minor literary subdivisions in references
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references set minor subdivisions and their abbreviations in lower-case (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules 37 and other numbering conventions; examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small initial letter for units of measurement abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial letters for units of measurement in abbreviation (h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second; lb.=pound, oz.=ounce; yd.=yard, ft.=foot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard abbreviations listed; use roman or small capitals as indicated elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize the first word and proper names; other words should be lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rules 172 and 280 for head styles and table heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not capitalize first word of a quotation connected to preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize the first word of a quotation if immediately connected with what precedes (unless beginning a sentence/paragraph in reduced type); similarly do not capitalize the first word after a colon when it's dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 35 and examples distinguishing closely connected quotations vs. independent quoted sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize words or phrases for emphasis and foreign insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to lend emphasis or to mark foreign-language insertions not anglicized; also single sentences or brief passages not lengthy enough for reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive example list of common foreign words/phrases (a priori, a posteriori, ennuI, café, résumé, bona fide, etc.). Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places commonly used in English; do not italicize anglicized words (percent, personnel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize titles of publications and long standalone works
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of publications — books (including plays and substantial poems printed separately), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals (including proceedings and transactions) and the name of a journal appearing in the journal itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; in newspapers the city name may be italicized when integral to the title. Cross-reference to rule 41 for capitalization in titles.
